text: MISERY IN PEKING.

label: paragraph_title
text:
PEOPLE'S DRIVEN TO
CRIME.

label: text
text: On account of the high cost of living and increase of unemployment resultant from the prolongation of the war, a large number of the poor people have been driven to the adventurous trade of robbery and burglary to gain a living. During the last two months over 100 cases of highway robbery have been reported around the metropolitan suburban districts. The majority of the robbers, were only armed with clubs, knives, or spears, while things robbed were of little value, such as horses, donkeys, clothes and sundries. This shows clearly that these robbers are not professional and only driven to this under desperate conditions.—Kuo Wen.

label: paragraph_title
text: CHINA COMMITTEE..

label: text
text: FORMER HONGKONG LAWYER A MEMBER.

label: text
text: The China Committee, the formation of which under the chairmanship of Lord Southborough our London correspondent announced in a recent letter, has now been enlarged and strengthened by the inclusion of Mr. Eugene Remsden, M.P., representing the Bradford Chamber of Commerce, Mr. J. Rankine, Edlayson and Mr. W. Maxwell Keekie, representing the Manchester Chamber of Commerce, and Mr. H. W. Looker, M.P., who was formerly a solicitor at Hongkong for many years, and now sits in the House of Commons as Member for the South-east Division of Essex. Our London correspondent writes that he is informed on the best authority that the formation of the China Committee is welcomed by the Foreign Office. It was set up by a group of Members of Parliament to watch over British interests in China and advise and assist the Government on matters connected with this country. It represents a multiplicity of interests outside politics which have connections with China, including the Federation of British Industries, the London Chamber of Commerce, the China Association, and many others. "Shanghai Times."

label: paragraph_title
text: Pancakes in the Menu.

label: text
text: Pannakes, as has so often been told, were in vogue in pre-Reformation days to use up the butter, cream, and eggs in the larder, these being forbidden foods during Lent. Recipes for pancakes are plenteous in the old cookery books. One edition I have of the famous Mrs. Hannah Glass's classic gives six recipes, four for those of "a fine sort." As the supposedly plain kind is generous of eggs and milk and contains a glass of brandy it was not exactly meagre (observes a writer in the "Daily Mail.") Another edition I have of Mrs. Glass's work contains nine pancake recipes, the last a "pink coloured one, a pretty corner dish for either dinner or supper." Bestroot juice is the colouring agent. Some of the old recipes meet the possibility of eggs being scarce. In that case the batter was made of flour, small beer, ginger, "etc." One I recall makes use of "clean snow." Sometimes the batter was fried in olive oil so that animal fat should not be used.

label: text
text:
PINCHEID FACE, OPEN EYES
OF TO-DAY.

label: text
text: Sir Harry Baldwin, surgeon-gentist to the King, lecturing at the Institute of Hygiene, made an unfavourable comparison of the face of the modern woman with that of a woman living in the Tudor period. Sir Harry said:

label: text
text: An examination of the wonderful portraits and drawing of personages of the Tudor period by Holbein, an Windsor Castle, will reveal that not one shows evidence of the contracted jaw pinched nostrils, and blankly gazing eyes of the adenoid subject.

label: text
text: For a typical example of a woman of the denoid diathesis, look in the exhibition of works by the late John Surgent now on view at the Royal Academy.

label: text
text: The eyes are wide open and expressionless; the whole nose, especially the region of the nostrils, is pinched and obviously inadequate to supply the requirements of normal nasal respiration; the mouth is somewhat open; the jaws are contracted and the teeth prominent. This woman is a well-marked example of what is characteristic of a great part of our nation at the present time.

label: text
text: Mr. Arthur Ponsonby, a member of the British aristocracy who joined the Labour Party and was a member of the first Labour Cabinet as Under-Secretary for Foreign Affairs, has now become an absolute pacifist. (His father was General the Right Hon. Sir Henry Ponsonby, and his mother was a granddaughter of Earl Grey.) Mr. Ponsonby recently published a book urging the people to refuse to take up arms in the next war, and he is now circulating copies of a letter to the Prime Minister, which he asks people to sign, containing the following pledge:

label: text
text: “We, the undersigned, convinced that all disputes between nations are capable of settlement either by diplomatic negotiations or by some form of International Arbitration, hereby solemnly declare that we shall refuse to support or render war service to any Government which resorts to arms.”

label: text
text: After being unable to walk for twelve years, Miss Bertha Johnston, of Newcastle, is now able to walk round her ward in the Loyal National Orthopaedic Hospital. Great Portland Street, W., with the aid of a stick. She has been suffering from infantile paralysis since the age of seven. Admitted to the hospital in March of last year, she has since undergone five operations and received other expert treatment, and recently the surgeons' success was first tested. She was taken from her bed and put on her feet, with a small knee support and crutches. A few days later she was walking round the ward.
